components.note: 身 — depicts a drawn bow
寸 — a hand releasing the arrow

example.hanzi: 科学家们成功发射了一颗卫星。
example.pinyin: Kēxuéjiāmen chénggōng fāshè le yì kē wèixīng.
example.english: The scientists successfully launched a satellite.
example.fact: 射's own components picture a drawn bow (身) plus a hand releasing the arrow (寸) — a vivid literal image of shooting that 发射 broadens from arrows to rockets, bullets, and even photons or radio waves ("to emit").

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.
冂 (an enclosure or doorway) — 内 pictures the space one enters.
人 (person) — a person entering an enclosure gave 内 its meaning 'inside' or 'within.'

example.hanzi: 这些问题必须在三天之内解决。
example.pinyin: Zhèxiē wèntí bìxū zài sāntiān zhīnèi jiějué.
example.english: These problems must be solved within three days.
example.fact: 之 is a classical, literary linking particle that functioned much like 的 — most of its old grammatical roles have faded from everyday speech, but it survives fossilized inside a handful of fixed formal compounds, including 之内, 之后 ("after"), and 之前 ("before").

components.note: 耂 (a variant of 老, 'old') — 考 relates to careful examination and testing
丂 gives a loose sound connection to 考's reading kǎo
讠 (speech) — 试 relates to proposing or trying something out
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 试's pronunciation shì

example.hanzi: 下星期我们有一场重要的考试。
example.pinyin: Xià xīngqī wǒmen yǒu yì chǎng zhòngyào de kǎoshì.
example.english: Next week we have an important exam.
example.fact: 考 alone already means "to test, to examine" and by extension "to ponder" (as in 思考), while 试 alone means "to try." 考试 layers one on top of the other — almost "to try at being tested" — a compositional logic that stays fairly transparent even to a learner meeting the word for the first time.

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.
子 (child/seed) — 存's meaning 'to exist, survive' has been linked to a seed persisting to grow.
才 (cái) gives a sound hint — 存 is pronounced cún, sharing the initial consonant though the vowel and tone differ.

example.hanzi: 在沙漠里生存非常不容易。
example.pinyin: Zài shāmò lǐ shēngcún fēicháng bù róngyì.
example.english: Surviving in the desert is not easy at all.
example.fact: 生存 pairs two verbs that each independently mean roughly "to live" — 生 ("to be born, to live") and 存 ("to exist, to remain") — the same reinforcing, double-up strategy behind words like 喜欢 and 应该. 生存 leans toward survival under threat or hardship, while the far more common 生活 is the neutral word for ordinary, everyday "life."

components.note: 犭 (dog) — 犯 originally related to a dog attacking, later extended to any act of violation
㔾 (jié) gives a sound distantly related to 犯's reading fàn, having drifted apart over time
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 警察正在追捕逃跑的犯人。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhèngzài zhuībǔ táopǎo de fànrén.
example.english: The police are chasing down the escaped convict.
example.fact: 犯 by itself is a verb meaning "to violate, to commit (an offense)," as in 犯法 ("to break the law") or 犯错 ("to make a mistake") — 犯人 simply adds 人 ("person") to name whoever did the violating, the same light noun-forming pattern behind 客人 ("guest") and 主人 ("host").

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — in the dark, one could not see a person's face, so calling out their name was necessary to identify them.
口 (mouth) — calling out with the mouth at night gave 名 its meaning 'name.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 这家餐厅接待过不少名人。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng jiēdài guò bùshǎo míngrén.
example.english: This restaurant has hosted quite a few celebrities.
example.fact: 名 literally means "name" but extends naturally to "fame, reputation" (as in 有名, "famous") — 名人 reads almost literally as "a name-person," someone whose name circulates widely, a similar image to how English "celebrity" traces back to Latin celeber, "thronged, famous."

components.note: 氵 (water) — 海 relates to bodies of water, specifically the sea.
每 (měi) gives a hint of the sound — 海 is pronounced hǎi, a connection that has shifted over time.
冖 here is a distorted form of 力 (strength) — a simplified way of showing soldiers grouped together.
车 (cart/vehicle) — 军 originally pictured soldiers riding out to battle in war chariots.

example.hanzi: 他哥哥在海军服役。
example.pinyin: Tā gēge zài hǎijūn fúyì.
example.english: His older brother serves in the navy.
example.fact: 军 alone means "army, military," and Mandarin names each service branch by pairing it with its domain: 海军 ("sea army" = navy), 陆军 ("land army" = army), 空军 ("air army" = air force) — a transparent, symmetrical naming system with no separate root words the way English has "navy," "army," and "air force."

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — ancient texts were written on bound bamboo strips, and 第 originally referred to the sequential order of such strips, giving rise to its meaning 'ordinal number' (as in 第一, first).
五 places an X-shaped cross between two horizontal lines representing heaven and earth — in traditional cosmology, this was linked to the five elements that fill the space between.

example.hanzi: 这是我今年读的第五本书。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ jīnnián dú de dìwǔ běn shū.
example.english: This is the fifth book I've read this year.
example.fact: 第 is a dedicated ordinal prefix with essentially no independent meaning outside this role — attach it to any cardinal number (一, 二, 三...) and it converts "one, two, three" into "first, second, third," functioning something like an English "-th" suffix, just placed in front of the number instead of after it.

components.note: 亻 (person) — represents a human figure.

叚 depicts borrowing or handing something over — a person who is not genuine, or something borrowed rather than real, gave 假 its meaning 'false, fake' (and, for a break from routine, 'vacation, leave.')
女 (woman) — depicts a wife in the traditional image behind this character.
口 (mouth/words) — the wife following her husband's spoken words gave 如 its meaning of 'as, like, if.'

example.hanzi: 假如我有很多钱,我会去世界各地旅行。
example.pinyin: Jiǎrú wǒ yǒu hěnduō qián, wǒ huì qù shìjiè gèdì lǚxíng.
example.english: If I had a lot of money, I would travel all over the world.
example.fact: 假如 sits at the more literary end of Chinese's "if" words — 如果 is the everyday default, while 假如 and its cousin 假使 feel a shade more formal or hypothetical, often signaling a scenario the speaker knows is unlikely or purely imagined, much like English "were I to..." versus plain "if I...".

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 结 relates to tying or knotting threads together.
吉 (jí) gives a hint of the sound — 结 is pronounced jié, a connection that has shifted over time.
尺 (a ruler/measure) — represents rules or measures being set.
口 (mouth) — measures being discussed aloud in one place gave 局 its meaning 'bureau, office, situation.'

example.hanzi: 这部电影的结局让人很意外。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng de jiéjú ràng rén hěn yìwài.
example.english: This movie's ending is quite surprising.
example.fact: 局 by itself covers a surprisingly wide range of senses — "bureau, office" (邮局, "post office"), "situation" (局面), and "a round of a game" (一局棋, "a game of chess") — 结局 draws on that last, game-like sense: literally "how the round tied off," i.e. how the story's game played out.

components.note: Depicts two things splayed apart from each other — such as a bird's two wings, or two people standing back-to-back — later used for the meaning 'not, contrary to.'
氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 非法停车会被罚款。
example.pinyin: Fēifǎ tíngchē huì bèi fákuǎn.
example.english: Illegal parking will be fined.
example.fact: 非 works here as a formal negative prefix meaning "non-, not-," attaching directly to a noun the way English "il-/non-" does — 非法 ("non-law" = illegal) sits alongside similar formal compounds like 非正式 ("informal") and 非常 ("extraordinary," literally "not ordinary").

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'

example.hanzi: 双方已经签了合同。
example.pinyin: Shuāngfāng yǐjīng qiān le hétong.
example.english: Both parties have already signed the contract.
example.fact: 合 alone means "to close, to fit together, to agree" and 同 alone means "same, together" — 合同 reads almost literally as "coming together in agreement," a fittingly on-the-nose etymology for the legal document that records exactly that.

components.note: 立 (to stand) pictures a person standing firm.
兄 (elder brother, here a rival) suggests standing up against someone, giving 竞 its meaning 'to compete, to contend.'
爪 and 彐 (two hands, reaching from opposite sides) — a simplified form of 爭, grabbing for the same thing.
亅 (the object) — what the two hands are struggling over, giving 争 its meaning 'to contend, compete, fight for.'

example.hanzi: 这两家公司之间的竞争非常激烈。
example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng jiā gōngsī zhījiān de jìngzhēng fēicháng jīliè.
example.english: The competition between these two companies is very intense.
example.fact: Both halves of 竞争 independently picture a contest: 竞's older form showed two rivals standing side by side (立 over 兄), while 争's form shows two hands (爪/彐) grabbing for the same object (亅) — 竞争 doubles up two already-vivid rivalry images into a single word.

meanings: youngster (often affectionate, of a child or animal)

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.
亻 (person) — 伙 relates to people who share meals or work together.
火 (huǒ) gives the sound — an exact match with 伙's reading huǒ.

example.hanzi: 这个小家伙才三岁,已经会自己穿鞋了。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiǎojiāhuo cái sān suì, yǐjīng huì zìjǐ chuān xié le.
example.english: This little guy is only three, and he can already put his own shoes on.
example.fact: 家伙 on its own is a casual, slightly rough word for "guy, fellow" (or even "tool, weapon," depending on context) — prefixing 小 ("little") softens it into an affectionate label, most often used for a child, a pet, or anyone small enough to be called "little" without any offense meant.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.hanzi: “对不起,我迟到了。”“没事儿,我们才刚到。”
example.pinyin: “Duìbuqǐ, wǒ chídào le.” “Méishìr, wǒmen cái gāng dào.”
example.english: "Sorry, I'm late." "It's fine, we just got here too."
example.fact: The retroflex -儿 ending on 没事儿 is a hallmark of colloquial, Beijing-flavored Mandarin — the same phrase written without it, 没事, is understood everywhere, but 没事儿 specifically signals a relaxed, informal register, the spoken cousin of the more neutral, all-purpose 没关系 ("it doesn't matter").

components.note: 爪 and 彐 (two hands, reaching from opposite sides) — a simplified form of 爭, grabbing for the same thing.
亅 (the object) — what the two hands are struggling over, giving 争 its meaning 'to contend, compete, fight for.'
又 (a hand) — reaching to take hold of something.
耳 (ear) — from an ancient battlefield practice of taking a fallen enemy's ear as proof of a kill, the origin of 取's meaning 'to take, obtain.'

example.hanzi: 我们要争取更多的时间。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yào zhēngqǔ gèng duō de shíjiān.
example.english: We need to fight for more time.
example.fact: 争取 always takes a concrete goal as its object — something you're actively working to secure, like 争取机会 ("to seek out an opportunity") or 争取时间 ("to buy time"). Its near-synonym 竞争 (also in this batch) frames the effort as a contest against a rival, while 争取 frames it as a reach toward a prize, with no opponent required.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 接 relates to receiving or connecting something by hand.
妾 (qiè) gives a hint of the sound — 接 is pronounced jiē, a connection that has shifted over time.
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 接下来,我们要讨论第二个问题。
example.pinyin: Jiēxiàlái, wǒmen yào tǎolùn dì èr gè wèntí.
example.english: Next, we're going to discuss the second question.
example.fact: 接下来 functions as a transition word opening a sentence, much like English "next" or "moving on." Its literal building blocks — 接 ("to receive, to connect") plus 下来 ("coming down, continuing on") — point to an older, more concrete sense of "taking up what comes next," which has since faded into a purely sequencing function word.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 人人都喜欢被称赞。
example.pinyin: Rénrén dōu xǐhuan bèi chēngzàn.
example.english: Everyone likes being praised.
example.fact: Reduplicating 人 into 人人 is one of Mandarin's simplest ways to build a universal quantifier ("every single person") with no extra grammar needed — the same doubling pattern shows up in 天天 ("every day," from 天, "day") and 家家 ("every household," from 家, "home").

components.note: A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'
Spirit — disasters were once thought to come from spirits or gods.
Gives the sound wō, related to huò but drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 昨天路口发生了一起车祸。
example.pinyin: Zuótiān lùkǒu fāshēng le yì qǐ chēhuò.
example.english: A car accident happened at the intersection yesterday.
example.fact: 祸 by itself means "disaster, misfortune," and shows up across a small family of calamity words — 灾祸 ("calamity," pairing it with 灾, "disaster"), 祸害 ("bane, scourge"), and the idiom 大祸临头 ("great disaster looming"). 车祸 is simply that general "disaster" root pinned to one specific cause: the automobile.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'

example.hanzi: 我们尝了很多当地小吃。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen cháng le hěnduō dāngdì xiǎochī.
example.english: We tried a lot of local snacks.
example.fact: 当 here means "the very one in question, this very" (as in 当时, "at that very time," or 当天, "that very day") rather than its other common sense, "to serve as" (当老师, "to work as a teacher"). 当地 leans on this less obvious reading to mean "this very place" — i.e., "local."

components.note: 上 (top) — the upper edge pressing down
卜 — the lower edge, with a card squeezed between the two

example.hanzi: 我用信用卡付了账。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yòng xìnyòngkǎ fù le zhàng.
example.english: I paid the bill with my credit card.
example.fact: 信用 on its own means "credit, trustworthiness" (信, "trust," plus 用, "to use" — trust that can be drawn on), while 卡 is a phonetic loan character borrowed purely for its sound (kǎ, echoing English "card"). 信用卡 is a clean split between a native Chinese compound and an imported, sound-based one.

components.note: 日 (sun) — represents the sun.
十 depicts the first rays of sunlight appearing low on the horizon — together with 日 (sun) giving 早 its meaning 'early, morning.'
日 (sun) — 晨 describes the time when the sun first rises, 'early morning.'
辰 (chén) gives the sound — an exact match with 晨.

example.hanzi: 他每天早晨都去跑步。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān zǎochén dōu qù pǎobù.
example.english: He goes running every morning.
example.fact: 早 and 晨 both independently mean roughly "morning, early," and both are built around 日 (the sun) — 早 shows the sun 日 with the first rays 十 breaking near the horizon, while 晨 pairs 日 with the phonetic 辰. 早晨 reinforces two sun-based dawn images into one everyday word for "morning."

components.note: 氵 (water) shows this relates to liquid, as in something boiling or rolling in water.
衮 (gǔn) gives the exact sound of 滚.
廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.hanzi: 水已经滚开了,可以下面条了。
example.pinyin: Shuǐ yǐjīng gǔnkāi le, kěyǐ xià miàntiáo le.
example.english: The water is already boiling, so we can put the noodles in.
example.fact: 滚开 leads a double life: said of water or another liquid, it's a neutral, everyday way to say "boiling," but shouted at a person it becomes a genuinely rude command to leave, on the same level as English "get lost" or worse — tone of voice and context do all the disambiguating work.

components.note: 夭 (a person leaning back) — the pose of someone laughing.
⺮ (bamboo-like strokes) — suggesting a wide grin, giving 笑 its meaning 'to laugh, smile.'

example.hanzi: 她对我微笑了一下。
example.pinyin: Tā duì wǒ wēixiào le yíxià.
example.english: She smiled at me briefly.
example.fact: 微 contributes the sense "slight, faint" (as in 微小, "tiny," or 微风, "a gentle breeze") to 笑 ("to laugh, to smile"). 微笑 is specifically the quiet, closed-mouth smile, set apart from a bigger, sound-making 大笑 ("to laugh out loud") by that one modifying character.

meanings: I, me (used to refer to oneself)

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.hanzi: 别管人家怎么想,做你自己觉得对的事。
example.pinyin: Bié guǎn rénjia zěnme xiǎng, zuò nǐ zìjǐ juéde duì de shì.
example.english: Don't worry about what other people think — do what you feel is right.
example.fact: 人家 hides two different words under one spelling. Read with a full tone on 家 (rén jiā), it's the literal, more formal "household, family." But in everyday speech, said with a light, neutral-toned jia (rén jia), it becomes a colloquial pronoun meaning "other people," "he/she/they," or even a coy stand-in for "I, me" — the reading pulled here is that common colloquial one, not the literal "household" sense.

components.note: 电 (simplified from 電) depicts a bolt of lightning — since lightning is a natural form of electricity, the character came to mean 'electricity.'
木 (wood) shows 梯 is typically made of wood.
弟 (dì) gives a sound close to tī, sharing a similar consonant sound though the vowel differs.

example.hanzi: 电梯坏了,我们只能走楼梯。
example.pinyin: Diàntī huài le, wǒmen zhǐnéng zǒu lóutī.
example.english: The elevator is broken, so we have to take the stairs.
example.fact: 梯 alone already means "ladder, steps" (as in 楼梯, "stairs") — 电 ("electricity") simply modifies it to name the powered version, the same modifying pattern behind 电话 ("electric speech" = telephone) and 电脑 ("electric brain" = computer).

components.note: 车 (cart) — 辈 originally described a row of chariots traveling together, extending to a 'group, generation' of people.
非 (fēi) gives a sound distantly related to bèi's reading, having drifted apart over time.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 他这辈子都没离开过这个小镇。
example.pinyin: Tā zhè bèizi dōu méi líkāi guò zhège xiǎozhèn.
example.english: He has never left this small town in his whole life.
example.fact: 辈子 almost always appears after a demonstrative — 这辈子 ("this lifetime"), 上辈子 ("a previous life," in a reincarnation sense), 下辈子 ("the next life") — rarely standing completely alone, since the word's whole job is to frame a span of time relative to one particular life.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'
口 is a simple picture of an open mouth.

example.hanzi: 紧急出口在这边。
example.pinyin: Jǐnjí chūkǒu zài zhèbiān.
example.english: The emergency exit is this way.
example.fact: 出口 splits into two logically connected but very different-feeling uses: literally "mouth of exit" for a physical doorway out of a building, and figuratively the same "going-out point" for goods leaving a country (to export) — the mirror-image word 进口 ("entrance" / "to import") extends the same in/out logic on both sides at once.

components.note: A drawing of a left hand holding a tool, contrasted with 又, an early form of the right hand.
辶 (walking/movement) — links 边's meaning to a boundary or edge one moves along.
臱 (biān) gives the sound — 边 is also pronounced biān, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 邮局就在银行的左边。
example.pinyin: Yóujú jiù zài yínháng de zuǒbian.
example.english: The post office is right on the left side of the bank.
example.fact: 边 as a suffix turns a direction into a location noun — 左 ("left") plus 边 gives "the left side," the same pattern behind 右边 ("right side"), 上边 ("above"), and 里边 ("inside"), a small, productive family of location words all built the same way.

components.note: 力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.hanzi: 警方还不清楚这起案件的动机。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng hái bù qīngchǔ zhè qǐ ànjiàn de dòngjī.
example.english: Police still aren't clear on the motive for this case.
example.fact: 机 ranges in meaning from "machine" (机器) to "opportunity" (机会) to, here, the more abstract "mechanism, trigger." 动机 reads almost literally as "the mechanism that sets something moving" — a fittingly mechanical image for whatever drives a person's actions.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, altar) — 礼 relates to ceremony and rites performed before the spirits.
乚 reflects the character's phonetic root, though its exact link to the modern reading lǐ is unclear today.
手 (hand), shown twice, side by side — two hands pressed together in a gesture of respect, giving 拜 its meaning 'to bow, to pay respects.'

example.hanzi: 下个礼拜我要去北京出差。
example.pinyin: Xià ge lǐbài wǒ yào qù Běijīng chūchāi.
example.english: Next week I have a business trip to Beijing.
example.fact: 礼拜 originally named the ritual of religious worship (礼, "rite," plus 拜, "to bow, to pay respects"). Because Christian services were traditionally held on Sunday, 礼拜 became colloquial shorthand for "Sunday" and then, by extension, for the whole seven-day "week" — a drift similar to how English "holiday" traces back to "holy day."

components.note: 黑 pictures a face or window blackened by soot rising from a fire 灬 below — giving 黑 its meaning 'black, dark.'
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.hanzi: 他穿了一件黑色的外套。
example.pinyin: Tā chuān le yí jiàn hēisè de wàitào.
example.english: He wore a black coat.
example.fact: 色 attaches to almost any basic color character to spell out its full name — 黑色 ("black"), 红色 ("red"), 白色 ("white") — but dropping 色 and using the bare color character alone (黑, 红, 白) is also grammatical and common, especially right before a noun, so learners see both forms constantly with no hard rule for which one to reach for.

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — in the dark, one could not see a person's face, so calling out their name was necessary to identify them.
口 (mouth) — calling out with the mouth at night gave 名 its meaning 'name.'
口 (mouth) — relates directly to 叫's meaning 'to call out, shout; to be named.'
丩 (jiū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jiào.

example.hanzi: 他名叫李明。
example.pinyin: Tā míngjiào Lǐ Míng.
example.english: He is named Li Ming.
example.fact: 名叫 is a slightly more written or formal way to introduce a name than the everyday spoken 叫 alone — 他叫李明 works just as well and is far more common in conversation — so 名叫 shows up more often in narration, biographies, and written introductions.

components.note: 欠 (to lack) shows 欺 relates to taking advantage of a lack or weakness in someone.
其 (qí) gives a sound close to qī, differing mainly in tone.
马 (horse) — 骗 originally described swinging up onto a horse, later extended figuratively to 'to trick, to swindle.'
扁 (biǎn) shares the rhyme -ian with piàn, and both use a bilabial initial (b/p) — only voicing and tone differ.

example.hanzi: 他欺骗了所有相信他的人。
example.pinyin: Tā qīpiàn le suǒyǒu xiāngxìn tā de rén.
example.english: He deceived everyone who trusted him.
example.fact: 骗 alone already means "to trick, to swindle." Its 马 (horse) component is a fossil of the character's original sense, "to spring up onto a horse" — a sudden, unexpected leap — later extended figuratively to catching someone off guard with a trick. 欺骗 reinforces that with 欺 ("to take advantage of, to bully").

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 控 relates to controlling or restraining something by hand
空 (kōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 控's reading kòng

example.hanzi: 这条街上到处都装了监控摄像头。
example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo jiē shàng dàochù dōu zhuāng le jiānkòng shèxiàngtóu.
example.english: Surveillance cameras have been installed all over this street.
example.fact: 监控 frequently doubles as a noun for the surveillance equipment itself, not just the abstract act of monitoring — 装监控 ("to install monitoring/cameras") and 看监控 ("to check the surveillance footage") are both everyday phrases where 监控 stands in for "the camera system," much like English "security" can mean both the concept and the guard.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 手机突然发出了奇怪的声音。
example.pinyin: Shǒujī tūrán fāchū le qíguài de shēngyīn.
example.english: The phone suddenly made a strange sound.
example.fact: 发出 pairs with almost any noun describing something radiating outward from a source — sound (声音), light (光), smell (气味), or a formal notice (通知) — functioning as a general-purpose "to emit / to issue" verb wherever English would reach for something more specific, like "to make," "to give off," or "to send."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拍 describes striking something lightly with the hand.
白 (bái) gives a sound distantly related to pāi, having drifted apart over time.
灬 (fire) — relates to 照's meaning 'to shine, illuminate; photograph.'
昭 (zhāo) gives a sound hint — 照 is pronounced zhào, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 我们在长城上拍照了。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài Chángchéng shàng pāizhào le.
example.english: We took photos on the Great Wall.
example.fact: 拍照 is a verb-object compound built from 拍 ("to strike, to tap" — the motion of pressing a shutter) plus 照 ("to shine, to photograph"). Because the object 照 is already baked into the verb, 拍照 cannot take a further object the way English "to photograph something" can — naming a subject requires a separate phrase, like 给...拍照 ("to take a photo of...").

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 船 is a vessel that travels on water, directly tied to its meaning 'ship, boat'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 船上有三百多名乘客。
example.pinyin: Chuánshàng yǒu sānbǎi duō míng chéngkè.
example.english: There are more than three hundred passengers on board the ship.
example.fact: 上 as a suffix after a place noun regularly means "on / at / in [that place]" — 船上 ("on the boat"), 桌上 ("on the table"), 车上 ("in the car") — one of Mandarin's most reliable location-building patterns, needing no preposition the way English "on," "at," and "in" would each have to be chosen separately.

components.note: 牙 (tooth) — teeth piercing or boring through something, the origin of 'to pierce'
穴 (xué) gives a sound distantly related to 穿's reading chuān, having drifted apart considerably over time
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.hanzi: 我们穿过了一条又长又黑的隧道。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen chuānguò le yì tiáo yòu cháng yòu hēi de suìdào.
example.english: We passed through a long, dark tunnel.
example.fact: 穿 alone already covers both "to wear (clothing)" and "to pierce, to pass through." 穿过 isolates and reinforces just the second, physical sense with 过 ("to cross over"), giving a verb specifically for moving through or across something — a tunnel, a crowd, or a forest.

components.note: 并 (simplified from 並) depicts two people standing side by side — giving its meaning of 'together' or 'and.'
Depicts two things splayed apart from each other — such as a bird's two wings, or two people standing back-to-back — later used for the meaning 'not, contrary to.'

example.hanzi: 他说的话并非事实。
example.pinyin: Tā shuō de huà bìngfēi shìshí.
example.english: What he said is by no means the truth.
example.fact: 并非 is a more emphatic, written-register stand-in for a plain 不是 ("is not"). The 并 adds a note of "contrary to what you might assume," so 并非 often appears right after a claim the speaker wants to correct or push back against — a rhetorical flavor a bare 不是 doesn't carry.

components.note: 彳 (to walk, step) — 彼 originally related to distance, extended to mean 'that, the other.'
皮 (pí) gives a sound close to bǐ.
寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.hanzi: 彼得是我在美国认识的朋友。
example.pinyin: Bǐdé shì wǒ zài Měiguó rènshi de péngyou.
example.english: Peter is a friend I met in America.
example.fact: 彼得 is a phonetic transliteration built purely for its sound — 彼 (bǐ) and 得 (dé) contribute nothing of the name "Peter"'s original meaning (from Greek petros, "rock"). This sound-first strategy is standard for foreign personal names rendered in Chinese, unlike native Chinese words, where the characters' own meanings usually matter.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 做 relates to a person carrying out an action.
故 (cause, reason, to happen) — combined with 亻 (person), 做 came to mean 'to make' or 'to do,' someone actively causing something to happen.
冖 (a roof/house) — the home being welcomed into.
友 (a friend) — brought close into one's home; the traditional form 愛 also includes 心 ('heart') in the middle — the source of 爱's meaning 'to love.'

example.hanzi: 医生说,怀孕期间做爱通常是安全的。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng shuō, huáiyùn qījiān zuò'ài tōngcháng shì ānquán de.
example.english: The doctor said that having sex during pregnancy is usually safe.
example.fact: 做爱 mirrors the English idiom "to make love" closely enough — 做 ("to do, to make") plus 爱 ("love") — that some learners assume one phrase was translated directly from the other; the two may simply have arisen independently, since "do/make + love" is a fairly natural image to reach for in more than one language.

meanings: to study at the same school

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'
冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.

example.hanzi: 我们是大学同学。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen shì dàxué tóngxué.
example.english: We're college classmates.
example.fact: 同学 does double duty as both a noun ("classmate") and, in spoken Mandarin, a generic form of address for a student whose name you don't know — a teacher or stranger can call out "同学!" much like English might use "excuse me" toward a young person on campus.

meanings: abbr. for 阿非利加洲[A1 fei1 li4 jia1 Zhou1]

components.note: Depicts two things splayed apart from each other — such as a bird's two wings, or two people standing back-to-back — later used for the meaning 'not, contrary to.'
氵 (water) — the water surrounding the land
州 (a stretch of land) — depicted as islands of land within a river

example.hanzi: 他去非洲旅行了三个月。
example.pinyin: Tā qù Fēizhōu lǚxíng le sān gè yuè.
example.english: He traveled around Africa for three months.
example.fact: 洲 is the dedicated character for "continent" and attaches to a single root syllable for each of the world's continents — 非洲 (Africa), 亚洲 (Asia), 欧洲 (Europe), 美洲 (the Americas) — all built the same transparent way, unlike English's unrelated continent names.

components.note: 言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
扌 (hand) — 报 relates to taking action against someone.
卩 (a kneeling or bound person) — handling a wrongdoer and announcing the judgment gave 报 its meaning 'to report' or 'to announce.'

example.hanzi: 空袭警报响了,大家都躲进了地下室。
example.pinyin: Kōngxí jǐngbào xiǎng le, dàjiā dōu duǒ jìn le dìxiàshì.
example.english: The air raid alarm went off, and everyone hid in the basement.
example.fact: 报 by itself means "to report, to announce" (as in 报纸, "newspaper," literally "report-paper") — 警报 combines it with 警 ("to warn, to alert") to mean, quite literally, "a warning announcement," the same logic behind 警察 ("police," literally "alert-observe").

meanings: (of a batter) to be put out (in baseball)
(of a player or team) to be eliminated from a competition

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'
尺 (a ruler/measure) — represents rules or measures being set.
口 (mouth) — measures being discussed aloud in one place gave 局 its meaning 'bureau, office, situation.'

example.hanzi: 这支球队在半决赛中出局了。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī qiúduì zài bànjuésài zhōng chūjú le.
example.english: This team was eliminated in the semifinals.
example.fact: 出局 borrows its core image from baseball and other turn-based games, where 局 means "a round, an inning" — so 出局 literally means "to go out of the round." A sports term for "eliminated," it has since spread into everyday talk about competitions, job cuts, and even politics.

components.note: 冂 (an enclosure or doorway) — 内 pictures the space one enters.
人 (person) — a person entering an enclosure gave 内 its meaning 'inside' or 'within.'
阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).

example.hanzi: 这份文件只在公司内部流传。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn wénjiàn zhǐ zài gōngsī nèibù liúchuán.
example.english: This document only circulates within the company.
example.fact: 内部 pairs 内 ("inside") with 部 ("section, department, part") to describe not just physical interiors but organizational ones too — 内部消息 ("inside information"), 内部矛盾 ("internal conflict") — a natural extension from physical space to institutional structure.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
贝 (shell, an ancient form of currency) — 质 originally meant 'pledge, hostage,' something valuable given as a guarantee, extended to 'quality, substance, nature.'
十 (shí) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zhì.

example.hanzi: 劫机者扣留了机上所有乘客作为人质。
example.pinyin: Jiéjīzhě kòuliú le jī shàng suǒyǒu chéngkè zuòwéi rénzhì.
example.english: The hijacker held all the passengers on the plane hostage.
example.fact: 质 can mean "pledge, guarantee" as well as "quality, substance" — its 贝 (shell, an ancient form of money) component is a fossil of that older "valuable pledge" sense. 人质 keeps this ancient meaning nearly intact: literally "a person held as a pledge," almost unchanged from the character's root meaning thousands of years on.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.hanzi: 请等我一会,我马上就回来。
example.pinyin: Qǐng děng wǒ yíhuì, wǒ mǎshàng jiù huílái.
example.english: Please wait for me a moment, I'll be right back.
example.fact: 一会 is often doubled into 一会儿一会儿 ("now this, now that") to describe rapid back-and-forth changes, as in 天气一会儿晴一会儿雨 ("the weather keeps swinging between sunny and rainy") — the same short-duration word repurposed to frame quick alternation, not just a single brief interval.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — dressing up and costuming traditionally involve the hands.
分 (fēn) gives a sound distantly related to bàn, having drifted apart over time.
氵 (water) — 演 originally described water flowing and spreading out, later extended to 'developing, unfolding'
寅 (yín) gives a sound distantly related to 演's reading yǎn, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 她在这部电影里扮演一位老师。
example.pinyin: Tā zài zhè bù diànyǐng lǐ bànyǎn yí wèi lǎoshī.
example.english: She plays a teacher in this movie.
example.fact: 扮 alone means "to dress up as, to disguise oneself as" (as in 打扮, "to get dressed up"), and 演 alone means "to perform, to act out." 扮演 combines "costuming" with "performing" into one verb, where English splits the same idea across "to play (a role)" and "to portray."
